title: Permutations and Combinations
prerequisites: Ability to multiply large numbers systematically.
Familiarity with the idea of an ordered pair.

topics.title: Fundamental Principle of Counting and Permutations
topics.quick_summary: If one task can be done in m ways and another in n ways, together they can be done in m × n ways; a permutation is an arrangement in which order matters.
topics.real_life: A four-digit PIN has 10,000 possibilities because each of the four positions independently has ten choices — the multiplication principle securing your bank account.

detailed.definition: The fundamental principle of counting states that if an event can occur in m ways and a second independent event in n ways, then both can occur in m × n ways. A permutation is an arrangement of objects in a definite order.
detailed.key_idea: Permutations count arrangements, so ABC and BCA are different. This is the one question to ask before choosing a formula: does the order matter?
detailed.working_principle: The number of permutations of n distinct objects taken r at a time is ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n−r)!. When all n objects are used, this becomes n!.
applications: Number of ways to seat 5 people in 5 chairs = 5! = 120.
Number of 3-letter words from 5 distinct letters = ⁵P₃ = 60.

points: Multiplication principle for 'and'; addition principle for 'or'.
Permutations of n objects where p are alike = n!/p!.
Circular permutations of n distinct objects = (n − 1)!.
mistakes: Taking 0! as 0; it is defined to be 1.
Adding when the tasks must both be done — 'and' means multiply.
Using n! for circular arrangements instead of (n − 1)!.
topics.memory_hook: 'AND means multiply, OR means add' — and 'Permutation = Position matters'.
topics.advanced: Circular arrangements lose one factor of n because rotating the whole circle produces the same arrangement. Whenever a symmetry maps arrangements onto each other, the count must be divided by the size of that symmetry group.

formulas.name: Permutations
formulas.variables: n = total number of distinct objects, r = number of objects taken at a time.
formulas.when_to_use: When order matters — arrangements, rankings, seatings, words from letters.
formulas.common_mistakes: Using it where order does not matter, which requires combinations instead.

topics.title: Combinations
topics.quick_summary: A combination is a selection in which order does not matter, and ⁿCᵣ = n!/[r!(n−r)!].
topics.real_life: A cricket selection committee choosing 11 from 15 players is making a combination — who is picked matters, the order of picking does not.

detailed.definition: A combination is a selection of objects without regard to order. The number of combinations of n distinct objects taken r at a time is ⁿCᵣ = n!/[r!(n−r)!].
detailed.key_idea: Every combination of r objects can be arranged in r! ways, so ⁿPᵣ = ⁿCᵣ × r!. Dividing permutations by r! removes the ordering, and that is the whole relationship between the two.
detailed.working_principle: The symmetry ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ holds because choosing r objects to include is the same as choosing n − r to leave out. It often halves the arithmetic.
applications: Selecting a committee, a team or a hand of cards.
The number of subsets of a set with n elements is 2ⁿ.

points: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ — choosing what to take is the same as choosing what to leave.
Sum of all ⁿCᵣ from r = 0 to n equals 2ⁿ.
mistakes: Using combinations for arrangements, where order matters.
Forgetting the r! in the denominator, which gives permutations instead.
Computing full factorials of large n instead of cancelling first.
topics.memory_hook: 'Combination = Committee (order irrelevant); Permutation = Podium (order decides everything).'
topics.advanced: The numbers ⁿCᵣ are exactly the entries of Pascal's triangle and the coefficients in the binomial expansion of (a + b)ⁿ. Counting, algebra and the triangle are three views of one object.

formulas.name: Combinations
formulas.variables: n = total objects, r = objects selected.
formulas.when_to_use: When order does not matter — teams, committees, subsets, card hands.
formulas.common_mistakes: Omitting r! in the denominator, which turns the answer into a permutation.
formulas.shortcut: Use ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ to pick whichever of r or n−r is smaller.
